title: Whoever is least (Luke 9:37–50)
hookLine: a boy healed, an argument about greatness, a child set beside him

lines: LOOK UPON MY SON: MINE ONLY CHILD.
cards: The next day they come down the mountain to a crowd, and a father shouting over the noise: "Master, I beseech thee, look upon my son: for he is mine only child."
Luke says a spirit seizes the boy, throws him into convulsions and leaves him bruised. And the father adds the painful part: "I besought thy disciples to cast him out; and they could not."
The disciples who stayed below have failed in front of everyone. Jesus' answer is weary, almost a sigh at the whole generation: how long shall I be with you? Then, simply: "Bring thy son hither."

teach.h: DELIVERED HIM AGAIN TO HIS FATHER.
teach.b: Even as the boy comes, he's thrown down again. Jesus rebukes the spirit, heals the child, and, in the King James words, "delivered him again to his father." Gave him back, the same gesture as the widow's son at Nain.

The crowd is "amazed at the mighty power of God." While everyone marvels, Jesus tells his disciples something hard: the Son of man will be delivered into human hands. They don't understand, and they're afraid to ask.

teach.h: WHICH OF THEM SHOULD BE GREATEST?
teach.b: Then, Luke says, "there arose a reasoning among them, which of them should be greatest." Right after failing to heal a boy. Right after hearing their teacher will be handed over.
Jesus knows what they're thinking, and answers without a speech.
He "took a child, and set him by him." Next to himself. They've been arguing about rank, and a child has none to offer.
"Whosoever shall receive this child in my name receiveth me: and whosoever shall receive me receiveth him that sent me: for he that is least among you all, the same shall be great."
Then John, a little too quickly: we saw someone driving out demons in your name, and we stopped him, because he isn't one of us.

teach.h: NOT AGAINST US IS FOR US.
teach.b: Jesus: "Forbid him not: for he that is not against us is for us."

teach.h: HE THAT IS LEAST AMONG YOU ALL, THE SAME SHALL BE GREAT.
teach.b: Two lessons in a row against the same instinct: to rank people, and to guard the circle.

how: Some churches point to Luke 9:48 in their work with children, from Sunday schools to child-protection and welcome policies, as a sign that receiving a child is receiving Jesus.

games.q: your friends are arguing about which of them is the greatest. you're their teacher. what do you do?
o: give a long talk on humility.
take a child, set the child beside you, and say the least is great.
name the greatest to end the argument.
games.why: Jesus doesn't argue. he sets a child next to himself and says whoever welcomes this child welcomes him.

practice: Picture Jesus setting a child next to him while the grown-ups go quiet, then think of a child in your life: your own, a neighbor's kid, a student, or the child you once were.

Let one need come clearly that's easy to overlook when adult things feel urgent: time, a ride, a bedtime story, a promise kept. If you pray, you can hold that child before God; if you don't, simply hold them in mind with care.

wordCard.voice: John. One of the twelve, who tried to stop a stranger driving out demons in Jesus' name, and was told forbid him not, on the day Jesus set a child beside him.

orig.note: Greek: smaller, lesser, least. "he that is least among you all."

carryVoice: Your line: the least is the greatest. A child with no rank gets the seat beside him. See you tomorrow.
